lesson.title: Good Stress, Bad Stress: Eustress vs. Distress
lesson.summary: Not all stress is harmful. Hans Selye distinguished eustress, stress that feels motivating and manageable, from distress, stress that feels overwhelming and damaging, even though both are genuine, real physiological stress responses.
lesson.body:
Building directly on the appraisal process from the previous chapter, whether a given stressor ends up feeling like eustress or distress often depends heavily on how it is appraised: as a challenge a person feels reasonably equipped to meet, or as a threat that outstrips their perceived resources to cope. Hans Selye, the researcher whose stage model of stress you will encounter in the general adaptation syndrome chapter, coined the term eustress specifically to capture that a stress response is not automatically a bad thing. A first day at a new job, training for a competition, planning a wedding, or working under a tight but achievable deadline can all activate the stress response while still feeling energizing, focusing, and even enjoyable in hindsight. Distress, by contrast, describes stress that feels overwhelming, uncontrollable, or damaging, such as a sudden job loss, an unresolved ongoing conflict, or a frightening medical diagnosis with no clear path forward.

It is worth being precise here: at the level of the body's physiological response, sympathetic activation, release of stress hormones, heightened arousal, eustress and distress can look remarkably similar in the moment. Both are real, biologically genuine stress responses, not one authentic reaction and one imagined one. The distinction lies less in a completely different bodily mechanism and more in duration, controllability, and the person's subjective appraisal of the situation. Related to this, the general idea that performance and functioning tend to improve with moderate arousal but decline once arousal becomes excessive, sometimes discussed as the Yerkes-Dodson law, is a related concept worth knowing, though it addresses performance under arousal specifically rather than the eustress-distress distinction itself.

The distinction matters practically because of what health psychology research has found: it is chronic distress, especially stress that feels prolonged and uncontrollable, that is consistently linked to negative health outcomes over time. Brief eustress, or a stressor appraised as a manageable challenge rather than an overwhelming threat, is not associated with that same cumulative wear, and can even sharpen motivation, engagement, and memory for the event. This is a genuine simplification worth flagging explicitly: individual differences, how long a stressor lasts, and how much control a person actually has all matter, and the line between eustress and distress is often fuzzy rather than a hard boundary.

Because appraisal drives so much of this distinction, the same event can shift categories over time or differ sharply between two people facing what looks, from the outside, like an identical situation, which is exactly what the transactional model of stress from the previous chapter would predict.
